To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the perception of briefly displayed objects is based on the recognition of their components, which are derived from the detection of the properties of edges.

the perception of objects in images is based on the detection of simple volumetric components and that the components are detected by a set of invariant image properties, namely, curvature, parallelism, symmetry, and coterminations.

the perceptual organization of a briefly presented image can be described in terms of a small number of volumetric components, and that the perception of objects is a process of componential recovery.

the question of how humans recognize objects from their images.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RBC is an empirically grounded, biologically plausible, and computationally tractable theory that provides a unified account for the major aspects of human object recognition.
RBC provides a unified account of a wide range of phenomena of object recognition and that the theory can serve as the foundation of a general theory of human vision.

RBC provides an account of object recognition that is consistent with the known properties of the human visual system and that has the potential for explaining the major phenomena of human visual recognition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual system does not recognize objects as a whole, but rather recognizes the object as a set of components.

object perception can be explained by a theory of recognition by components, which assumes a small set of primitive volumetric components, and that this theory provides a unified account of object recognition in terms of a few simple principles.
